lead: Use an AI video generator for ecommerce to turn a photo or product page into a short product clip. Choose a video type, set the frame and length, then describe the scene.
card: Short video ads, demos and unboxings made from one product photo.

intro: Choose a video direction for the product moment you want to show: a creator-style ad, a product demonstration, an unboxing, a visible change, or motion added to a still photo. Start from a product photo or a product page link, then describe one clear action.
Choose a 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9 frame and a length of 6, 10, or 15 seconds. Each run makes one clip, and the credit cost appears before you start.

benefits.d: A single clear product shot is enough to begin. No photo handy? You can start from a written description instead.
Vertical, square, and wide formats are built in, so you never have to squeeze a wide clip into a TikTok frame.
The credit cost appears before a job starts. When a video fails, those credits go straight back to your balance.

faq.q: Do I need a product photo to make a video?
faq.a: No, but it helps. With a photo, the video is built around your actual product. Without one, the result comes from your description alone, so it may not match your item exactly.

faq.q: How long are the videos, and what sizes can I choose?
faq.a: You can pick 6, 10, 15, or 30 seconds. Formats include 9:16 vertical, 1:1 square, and 16:9 wide, plus 3:4 and 4:3.

faq.q: Can I add my price, captions, or music?
faq.a: Add those after you download. Put prices, dates, and discount codes on in Canva, CapCut, or Ads Manager, and add captions and music in TikTok or CapCut. AI-generated text can come out misspelled, so it's safer to type it yourself.

faq.q: What does one video job cost?
faq.a: The displayed cost depends on length: 6 seconds uses 24 credits, 10 uses 40, 15 uses 60, and 30 uses 120. The workspace currently exposes 6, 10, and 15 seconds.

faq.q: What should the first shot of a product video show?
faq.a: Show the item clearly before it moves. Use one action that explains its purpose, and keep the label and important parts in view as the scene develops.

overview.h2: Choose the video type for your product
overview.p: A demonstration can show one useful action. An unboxing can reveal what comes in the package. A creator-style ad can frame a quick product moment, while image-to-video adds movement to a still photo.

overview.h2: Set the format before you start
overview.p: Use 9:16 for a vertical feed, 1:1 for a square placement, or 16:9 for a wide video area. Pick 6, 10, or 15 seconds to match the space where you plan to use the clip.

input_guide.h2: Prepare one product photo that can carry the scene

items.d: Use a product shot where the complete shape, main color, and important parts are visible instead of cropping away the feature you want to show.
A little space around the product gives camera movement and hand actions somewhere to happen without cutting into the object.

items.t: Match the photo to the job
items.d: Choose a clean hero shot for motion, a feature view for a demo, and a packaging reference when the box or insert is part of the story.
Name one place, one main action, and one product detail. A single focused moment is easier to judge than a list of unrelated scenes.
Decide on vertical, square, or wide before you describe the composition so the framing fits the place where you will post it.
A quick clip for one short product moment.
Room for a simple action or reveal.
More time to show a product in use.
A hand pulls a stainless water bottle from a canvas gym bag beside a bench, then turns it toward the light.
A lunch box sits on a kitchen counter while its lid clicks shut and the front latch locks into place.
A matte black mailer opens on a pale table, tissue folds back, and a candle is lifted into view.
A crowded entryway with loose shoes changes to the same space with pairs lined up on a bamboo rack.
Morning light travels across a watch on a stone surface as the camera makes a slow, close push toward the face.
A compact speaker rests on a desk beside a laptop while a hand reaches in to turn the dial.
Add the price, date, discount code, or product name yourself so every small character matches the approved source.
Add captions, music, or a voiceover in TikTok, CapCut, Ads Manager, or your usual editor after download, since the generated clip doesn't include them.

items.t: Review the clip from first to last frame
items.d: Look for changes to labels, colors, edges, or small parts before publishing and keep the version that represents the item honestly.
Name files by product, scene, shape, and date so a later test does not overwrite the opening you want to reuse.
Add the live stock status and offer conditions from your seller record, then verify them again before scheduling; inventory or deadlines may change after a scene is prepared.

good: Small stores testing several product angles from an approved photo
Catalog teams that need short visual demos for different placements
Launch teams preparing a reveal before a full shoot is scheduled
Sellers who want product-specific scenes instead of a generic text overlay
not_ideal: Claims that depend on an exact medical, body, or performance transformation
Scenes where tiny printed text must remain perfectly accurate throughout

compare.h2: How this fits with other ways to make a clip

items.d: You begin with one product photo and a written scene, so there is no camera setup or location schedule inside the process.
You can test several openings from the same product reference without arranging sample shipping or a creator brief.
A clip can show an action, reveal, or change that a single frame cannot communicate by itself.
The generated file is a starting visual; your team still controls the final wording, sound, placement, and approval.

scene_prompt_examples.h2: Turn a broad idea into a clear shot

items.d: Broad: “Show this jar.” More specific: “A hand turns the glass moisturizer jar on a pale vanity; tight product framing, soft morning light from the right.” This names one movement, one place, the distance of the shot, and the light source, so the jar stays in focus.

Broad: “Show my backpack.” More specific: “A hand pulls the zipper on a navy daypack beside an open train seat; medium close-up, window light across the fabric.” The action and setting tell viewers what to look at, while the framing gives the bag more attention than the passing background.

Broad: “Make a video of my tea.” More specific: “A round tea tin turns on a wooden breakfast table beside a cup; close framing, side light through a kitchen window.” The concrete direction sets the location, the change in the scene, and which product details should stay in view.

Broad: “Show how this speaker works.” More specific: “A finger presses the top dial on the speaker at a desk; tight shot, cool daylight from a side window.” One visible gesture gives the scene a clear subject and beat instead of leaving a long sequence open to interpretation.

troubleshooting.h2: Make one focused change when a result misses

items.d: Switch to a straight-on photo that shows the whole item, then simplify the scene to one small movement. Compare the result with the actual product before using it.
Keep exact words out of the visual direction. Use a clean product view, then add verified brand, ingredient, or offer wording in your editor after download.
Describe one starting position and one visible action, such as a lid closing. If two movements compete, split them into separate clips or try the Product Videos tool for a single feature.
Ask for a close shot with the item in the foreground and drop extra props from the description. Fewer objects leave more of the frame for the product.
